title: Gibraltar's New Deal with the EU: Sovereignty, Borders, and Beyond
label: 15 September 2026 · Gibraltar treaty scrutiny
summary: The European Affairs Committee questioned Lord Wood of Anfield and Paul Hughes about the UK-EU agreement on Gibraltar. They explained why Gibraltar was excluded from the 2020 trade deal, how the new treaty aims to keep the border fluid, and the complex governance arrangements. Key issues included protecting UK sovereignty, military autonomy, Schengen checks, and termination clauses. The witnesses stressed that Gibraltar chose these arrangements and that sovereignty is unaffected, but some members challenged whether Spain gains too much influence.

chapters.title: Why Gibraltar Needed a Separate Deal
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar was left out of the 2020 trade deal, so a bespoke treaty was needed to keep the border open and avoid economic disruption.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Minister, why wasn't Gibraltar included in the 2020 trade and co-operation agreement? And why did it take five years to get this new agreement?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Gibraltar wasn't in the TCA because the EU, probably pushed by Spain, wanted separate arrangements. The bridging measures that followed kept the border fluid informally, but they weren't sustainable. Businesses couldn't plan, and the EU's new entry/exit system meant Spain couldn't keep them going. So we needed a treaty.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Why five years? First, it's complex—over 1,000 pages, many dossiers, physical infrastructure. Second, politics: we had turmoil in the UK in 2022, a Spanish election in 2023, and a change of government here in 2024. That slowed things down.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: You talk about 'fluidity at the frontier'. How is that different from free movement?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Fluidity means the 15,000 people who cross the land border daily can do so without checks. That's the key to Gibraltar's economy. It's not free movement—there are different arrangements for air and sea arrivals.

chapters.title: Sovereignty: Red Lines and Reassurances
chapters.takeaway: The treaty explicitly protects UK sovereignty over Gibraltar, and any alignment with EU rules is a choice by Gibraltar, not a concession.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The treaty involves dynamic alignment with EU rules. Does that threaten UK sovereignty, especially with Spain getting powers over arrest, residency, and borders?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: No, sovereignty isn't diminished. Article 2 explicitly says the treaty doesn't affect the sovereignty position. These are technical arrangements about Gibraltar's relationship with the EU. Gibraltar chose to align in certain areas to get the benefits of an open border.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: But you said there are 43 annexes of EU law applying to Gibraltar. That sounds like a lot.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Actually, most of those annexes aren't about EU law—they're procedural or lists. Only about eight contain EU law references, and Gibraltar opted into those. It's a bespoke deal that avoids imposing irrelevant EU law.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What about Spain's role? Could it creep into more control over Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: No, the scope is carefully delineated. For example, Spanish military officers only deal with military derogations and limited information sharing. There's no jurisdiction for them to expand. In fact, more cooperation is what makes the treaty work.

chapters.title: Military Base and Schengen Checks
chapters.takeaway: The treaty protects UK military operational autonomy, with special arrangements for personnel and goods, and Schengen checks won't trap military staff in the 90-day rule.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Will this treaty affect military personnel and access to the naval base?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Safeguarding operational autonomy was a red line. There's no Spanish role in authorising UK military operations or deployments. Military personnel, civilians on defence business, and their families aren't subject to routine Schengen checks.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: We do have limited information sharing with Spanish military liaison officers to facilitate military derogations. The Commander British Forces is positive about how it's working.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What about the Schengen 90-day rule? Could military staff get caught up in that when visiting other Schengen countries?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: There's now an arrangement so military personnel can clock in and out, stopping and starting the Schengen clock appropriately. That's an implementation improvement in the last couple of months.

chapters.title: Entry Decisions and Mutual Recognition
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar keeps control over who enters, but it has agreed to mutually recognise Spanish refusals into Schengen based on security concerns, which raised questions about what happens if the two disagree.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Who decides who can be refused entry into Gibraltar? Could Spain effectively block someone?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Gibraltar has been in charge of entry for decades, and that continues. Gibraltar residents can't be refused entry. Everyone arriving at the airport goes through Gibraltar immigration, then Spanish Schengen checks.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: If someone is flagged in the Schengen Information System, Spain may refuse them entry into Schengen. Gibraltar has decided to mutually recognise those refusals based on security or public safety. But Gibraltar still makes its own decision about entry into Gibraltar.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So if Gibraltar says no but Spain says yes, what happens? Could someone be allowed into Spain but not Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Conceptually, yes. Gibraltar controls entry to Gibraltar. But we'll get back to you on the specific case of non-residents. The Chief Minister can also give you a practical answer.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That's an important point—please do come back to us with clarity.

chapters.title: Costs, Concordat, and Termination
chapters.takeaway: The UK won't pay for the financial mechanism—Gibraltar will—and the concordat is a political, not legal, document; termination clauses include a Spanish option only after a four-year review.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: How much will Gibraltar pay for this, and will the UK contribute?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Both parties will set up independent funds. Gibraltar will fund its own, and under the concordat, the UK contribution will come from Gibraltar, not UK taxpayers. No specific timelines yet, but it'll be set up soon.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What's the legal status of the concordat? Is it as binding as the treaty?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: It's a political agreement, not legally binding. It sets out how the UK and Gibraltar will work together on implementation. It respects constitutional arrangements and was wanted by Gibraltar.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: It's a political instrument between us and the Government of Gibraltar.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So it can be changed by political whim. That's a contrast to the treaty's enforcement mechanisms.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Any UK Government will want a good relationship with Gibraltar, and Gibraltar will want clarity. So I expect it to endure.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: On termination: there seem to be three routes—Article 334 with 12 months' notice and Gibraltar consent, Article 19.5 with 90 days if Gibraltar rejects an EU law update, and Spain unilaterally forcing termination. Is that right?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Article 19.5 is precedented in EU agreements with Norway, Switzerland, and Iceland. It's for a very specific scenario where Gibraltar rejects an update, triggering a 90-day discussion period. It's designed to be resolved.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: The Spanish option is in the mobility chapter, after a four-year review. If Spain tells the EU it's no longer content, the EU can start termination. It's not at any time—it's tied to that review.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is it a one-off option at that moment?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: I'm fairly certain, yes. We can confirm with the Chief Minister.

chapters.title: The Road Ahead
chapters.takeaway: The treaty is the final piece of the Brexit puzzle, providing a stable foundation, but implementation will require ongoing cooperation and adjustments.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Does this agreement settle Gibraltar's future for good, or will more agreements be needed?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: From a treaty perspective, it's the last piece of the jigsaw after Brexit. Sovereignty is fully protected. There will be implementation adjustments, but this is a stable and lasting foundation for Gibraltar's relationship with the EU.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both for your evidence. We're on time. It's been a pleasure.
